newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS -Delta's new CEO no stranger to competition.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -Delta's new CEO no stranger to competition.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc's new chief executive officer and president Leo Mullin may be a stranger to the airline industry, but he is no stranger to the customer service woes and competitive concerns that remain Delta's biggest challenges, analysts said.
Mullin succeeds Ronald Allen, who left the nation's third largest airline after 34 years amid a clash with the board about sinking employee morale and customer satisfaction.
Mullin's appointment marks the first time the nation's third-largest airline hired an outsider as CEO.
"I think he's going to breathe new life into Delta and really bring new ideas to the table, which is something Delta needs," Susan Donofrio, an airline analyst at NatWest Securities Corp.

Mullin's background in utilities, banking and railroads -- where he has seen competitive pressures intensify amid loosening government regulation -- makes him well-suited for the airline industry, analysts said.
After years of instability that followed the deregulation of the airline industry, carriers are seeing record profits and intense competition.
Airlines also are bracing for an expected move toward consolidation and increasing pressure from low-cost carriers.
Mullin hails from Chicago-based Unicom Corp, the parent of utility Commonwealth Edison Co, where he also was tapped to bring a new perspective to an industry bracing for deregulation and competition.

"The reason he joined Unicom is to bring an outside opinion and viewpoint and more competitive idea on how Unicom should go in a new era of deregulation," said Daniele Seitz, a utilities analyst with UBS Securities.
"He was there to give a of view of an outsider ... instead of hanging on to the old rules. He brought an era of fresh air."
In less than two years at Unicom, Mullin focused on cost-cutting, trimming employees and upgrading core operations. "It was a very tough period of self-examination," Seitz said.

Before joining Unicom, Mullin was president of bank holding company First Chicago Corp. Preceding his 14-year career there, Mullin worked at Conrail Corp as a strategic planner following rail industry deregulation.

Mullin said he was ready to tackle the close-knit airline industry. "I think there will be a learning curve, but I do not think it will be steep," Mullin said, referring to his ability to acclimate to varied industries such as railroads, banking and utilities.
"I don't think that not having grown up in the industry is a barrier to strong performance," said Timothy Ross, an airline analyst with SBC Warburg.
Mullin's biggest challenge will be to improve Delta's customer service reputation while monitoring costs, analysts said.

"They need to not give up the incredible cost-cutting progress they made in the past," said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read. "But they need to strike a balance between controlling costs and service."

During Allen's tenure, Delta returned to profitability from huge losses in the early 1990s after undergoing a massive cost-cutting program that raised operating efficiencies and trimmed 15,000 jobs from the airline's payroll.
But the three-year cost-cutting program rattled Delta, leaving its once-robust employee spirit and customer service tradition in an anemic state.
Delta has been losing premium business traffic for years because of worsening customer service, at a time when its rivals have focused closely on wooing high-paying corporate travelers.

Customer satification surveys show "there has been some erosion in the customer satisfaction. There's no denial ... within this company with respect to the necesity to tackle that as an early and top priority," Mullin said.
Mullin said he sees Delta's customer service as "bent, not broken."
"We've had similar customer service difficulties at times in those places. And the important thing is to get a clear understanding of cause and effect and attack it," he said.
Mullin's fresh view on Delta will be paired with the extensive airline experience of other top executives named Friday.

Delta named Gerald Grinstein, a member of Delta's board and head of the CEO search committee, as non-executive chairman of the board. Maurice Worth, acting Delta CEO, was named chief operating officer. Mary Johnston Evans, acting chairman, was named chairman of the executive committee of the board.

"This new leadership gives Delta shareowners, employees and customers a mix of airline industry experience and a new and objective management approach with a proven record of achievement," Grinstein said.
